archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A thick-framed improviser whose value comes from breaking the pocket and running for first downs, while a shaky, inaccurate arm caps what Miami's passing game can be.

report.headline: His legs keep Miami afloat; his arm, especially deep, keeps sinking them.
report.take:
Malik Willis is finally getting the starter's runway he never had in Tennessee or Green Bay, and six starts in, the picture is clear. He is a real runner and a below-par passer. His 223 rushing yards rank 2nd among 45 qualifying quarterbacks. His passing ranks near the bottom: -0.105 EPA per dropback (35th), a -7.17 CPOE (40th) and a 9.6% sack rate (39th). Miami is 1-5 and passes far less than the situation calls for (pass rate over expected -10.5, 31st). That reads as a staff that knows what it has and is hiding the arm behind the run game.

The key to his season is that his scrambles pay for his mistakes. His charted passing EPA adds up to -17.5, but all 189 dropbacks combined, scrambles included, come to just -1.2. Twenty-two scrambles at 0.897 EPA each, 12 of them for first downs, nearly cancel out the sacks, the misfires and the fumbles. That trade is who he is: his career pressure-to-sack rates ranked at or near the bottom in every season, so the long holds (3.13 seconds to throw) and the sacks come with the creation. The designed runs are a different story. At 1.91 yards a carry with a 36.4% stuff rate, they don't work, so his rushing value is improvised, not schemed.

The passing profile is lopsided in a revealing way. Short throws (0.189 EPA, 55% success) and intermediate throws (0.355 EPA) have been fine to good. The damage comes at both extremes: throws behind the line have bled -9.9 EPA, and deep balls have connected only 20.7% of the time with a -18.1 CPOE. Shotgun dropbacks (-0.191 EPA) have been far worse than under-center ones (0.063). That points the same direction: he is better when play-action and the run game set things up than when he has to win from a spread look. His target tree splits sharply too. Greg Dulcich (0.555 EPA per target) and Caleb Douglas (0.841) have produced, while Kevin Coleman Jr.'s 18 targets sank -13.3 EPA, a hole worth closing by simply throwing elsewhere.

The gaudy 2024-25 Green Bay lines (an 85.7% completion rate and a 22 CPOE last year) came over two or three games each and were never his true level. The 2022 rookie line was ugly in the other direction. This season, on real volume, sits in between and is the most honest read yet. The Week 7 win over the Jets, coming off the bye, showed the formula at its best: a 5.1-yard intended air distance, 14 of 21 passing, 11.4 passing EPA and 37 rushing yards. That is a game plan, not a breakout. Expect it to be repeated against weak coverage and to fail against good rushes.

strengths.title: Scrambles that erase his sacks
strengths.body: His scrambles are the most valuable plays in Miami's offense, averaging 0.897 EPA, with more than half moving the chains. They come from the same instinct that produces his sacks: holding the ball to extend plays. They also carry his dropbacks from deeply negative to roughly neutral. This has shown up in every stint of his career and should hold.

strengths.title: Short-to-intermediate passing works
strengths.body: Between the line and 19 air yards, he has been a functional passer. Throws of 0-9 yards succeed more than half the time, and 10-19 yard throws carry strong EPA despite middling accuracy. The intermediate figure rests on just 31 attempts and likely runs a little hot. Still, it tells the staff where the passing game lives, and the Jets win showed they know it.

strengths.title: Two targets who produce
strengths.body: Dulcich and Douglas have turned their targets into real value. Dulcich in particular gives him a reliable middle-of-the-field outlet, which suits a quarterback who is accurate over the middle (0.2 CPOE) and erratic outside the numbers. Feeding these two more often, and Coleman less, is the easiest passing upgrade available.

concerns.title: Accuracy collapses down the field
concerns.body: One in five deep throws has been completed, and his CPOE overall ranks 40th. A 15.9% bad-throw rate says this is mostly ball placement rather than receivers failing him. The 2022 Titans numbers looked similar, so it is likely a genuine limit, not a slump. It caps his ceiling as a passer.

concerns.title: Sacks and fumbles kill drives
concerns.body: The sacks are partly the price of his scrambling. Even so, a 9.6% rate is costly, especially with seven sacks on third down and four in the red zone. The fumbles are the bigger flaw: three lost, ranking 42nd of 45, on five turnover-worthy fumbles. Some of the lost-fumble count is bounce luck, but ball security while extending plays is a real issue.

concerns.title: Shotgun and screen game sputter
concerns.body: When Miami spreads him out, the offense craters, and throws behind the line have been a steady drain despite a 75% completion rate. That points to a quick game that isn't creating yards. Some of it is scheme and receiver quality, but it limits how often Miami can build around him from shotgun.

trend.note: His passing EPA has swung from 4.5 at San Francisco to -12.4 at Minnesota and -11.4 against Cincinnati, then to a season-best 11.4 against the Jets after the bye. Opponent quality explains part of it: the Vikings rank 1st on defense today, while the Jets sit 17th. The last three games still rate worse per dropback than his season (-0.172).

nextGame.headline: Average Patriots defense, thin secondary, but a likely chase script.
nextGame.body:
New England's defense is middle of the pack: 16th in EPA, 17th against the pass, and 23rd in deep EPA allowed, so this is not the Minnesota wall. Its pass rush is solid, 12th in sack rate and 10th in hit rate, which is where Willis's sack-taking gets tested. The Patriots have been stingy against tight ends (-0.06 EPA per play, 6th), the role Dulcich fills. Their WR1 numbers conflict: generous per play but under average in fantasy points. The bigger issue is script. The Book has NE -7.5 with Miami at +310, and Miami's league-worst pass defense meets the league's 5th-best passing offense. Willis may have to throw more than this run-leaning staff wants.

Availability tilts toward Miami's passing game. Carlton Davis III, a 95%-snap starting corner, is out, and so are depth corners Channing Canada and Karon Prunty. New England will be leaning on thin coverage behind its top layer. On the other side, the Patriots' offense is missing guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (IR) and center Ben Brown. That could slow their run game, which already ranks 28th, and keep the game closer than the line suggests. Miami's only listed injury, RB Jaylen Wright (questionable, 14% of snaps), is a depth piece and doesn't change Willis's day.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Patriots corners
keyMatchups.body: With Davis out along with two depth corners, New England's coverage is at its thinnest. This is the kind of week where Willis's intermediate throws, his best zone, and an occasional shot to Douglas can land. It doesn't fix his deep accuracy, but it widens the windows.

keyMatchups.title: Pass rush vs his holds
keyMatchups.body: New England gets home at an above-average clip, and Willis holds the ball longer than most. Every extended play becomes a coin flip between a scramble first down and a sack or strip. Which side wins that flip decides his game.

keyMatchups.title: Chase script from Miami's defense
keyMatchups.body: Miami's pass defense ranks last, and New England's passing offense ranks 5th. If the Patriots go up two scores, Miami's run-first plan breaks down. His trailing-by-9-plus split (-0.13 EPA) shows he doesn't feast in catch-up mode.

nextGame.watch: Whether the staff repeats the Jets plan of quick, short throws, or whether a deficit forces him into the shotgun and deep-ball dropbacks where he has struggled most.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect what he has been, with a bit of smoothing. The rushing floor is sustainable: scrambles are a career-long trait, and his roughly 37 rushing yards a game should hold in the 30-45 range, with goal-line and scramble touchdowns keeping his fantasy line steadier than his passing. The passing should stay below average. A low-volume, run-first offense and a deep game that rarely connects cap him around 150-200 yards a game. The touchdown rate, well under the league's, has some room to rise as Dulcich and Douglas earn more looks. The lost fumbles should cool somewhat, since part of that is bounce luck.

The risk is game script. Miami's defense is among the league's worst, so more games may tilt into catch-up passing, where he is least effective. A heavier diet of play-action, under-center work and the middle of the field is his best version, and the Week 7 win suggests the staff knows it. Don't mistake that game for a new baseline, but don't mistake the Minnesota dud for one either.
swingFactors: How often Miami falls behind early and has to pass
Sack and fumble control on extended plays
Targets shifting toward Dulcich and Douglas

confidence.note: The six-start sample is consistent and matches his career rushing traits, but the depth splits are small and the opponent swings are large.
